newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Argentine deal enables Bilbao to expand in retail.
newsitem.headline: Argentine deal enables Bilbao to expand in retail.

text.p: Spain's Banco de Bilbao Vizcaya's move to acquire control of a major Argentine retail bank fits snugly into its strategy of widening its Latin American retail services to strengthen its position in the region, analysts say.

They spoke after the BBV-controlled Banco Frances in Argentina caught markets by surprise with the announcement last Friday of a deal to buy a 71.8 percent stake in retail banker Banco de Credito Argentino.

Frances did not disclose the deal's value but banking sources put it at some $430 million. They added BBV, which has a 30 percent controlling stake in Frances, is negotiating to buy all the shares of Credito for a total of about $600 million.
"The purchase is part of a BBV strategy to launch retail services they are specialized in," said Carlos Gomez-Lopez, analyst of Latin American banks for Paribas.

"BBV is trying to expand its retail business, its key feature, in other countries. For example it has a savings account with raffle related gifts," he said. "BBV launched it in Spain and last year in Mexico with a lot of success."

Jorge Scarinci, analyst for Robert Fleming, said "BBV is very aggresive in retail business. They are doing the same in other countries like Peru and Colombia." He added the deal price would be reasonable up to $450 million.
Frances is Argentina's third largest private bank after Galicia and Rio. Banco de Credito Argentino ranks as one of Argentina's 10 retail banks.
Analysts said an acquisition of Banco de Credito looked like a good complement to BBV's already-existing Argentine holdings.
"It would be an excellent deal for Frances," Gomez-Lopez said. "In case it goes ahead we will be upgrading our Frances rating from hold to buy."
Frances clients are mainly big companies and high income individuals while Credito is more a retail banking with strong presence in the mid-to-low income segment.

Alberto Sanchez, analyst for Bear Stearns, said BBV was trying to expand its retail business and the deal suited it like a ring around a finger. "This solves it all of one fell swoop. In general terms it puts BBV in an enviable situation."
But he cautioned there would be some branch overlap in the short term and a subsequent restructuring could be expected.
"In a bank merger two plus two never equals four, mostly in the first 18 months," Sanchez said. "After that they equal four and even five."

He added the deal puts a lot of presure not only over other local banks like Galicia, Rio and Bansud but also over Spain's Santander to expand in Argentina, where it has only an investment bank presence. "They have to buy something in Argentina not to be left out of the market."
Nuno Fernandes, of ING Barings, said despite some branch overlap and likely closures, the bank could avoid losing clients.
"Frances has the profile to keep them. The question is how long it will take it to restructure. If it delays too much it would be bearing the higher costs over that period."
Referring to the cost of the deal, Fernandes said "if it turns to be about $400 million I deem it reasonable, but not much more above that."
